canberra.title: Generational Canberrans: A border divided their farm, but 188 years of history unite the Southwells
canberra.snippet: For most people, the border between the ACT and NSW is little more than a line on a map. For Kingsley Southwell, it once ran straight thr...
canberra.content:
Kingsley Southwell displays his family tree, tracing its history to 1838, with records preserved since 1942. Photo: Naziya Alvi. Kingsley with his granddaughter, continuing a family legacy in the Canberra region dating back to 1840. Photo: Supplied.

For most people, the border between the ACT and NSW is little more than a line on a map. For Kingsley Southwell, it once ran straight through his family’s farmland.

One part of the property was in the ACT; the other in NSW. And although the land had been farmed by generations of his family, the boundary meant it was subject to two different systems of land ownership.

“There were 200 acres in the ACT and 24 in NSW because the border went through one corner of it,” the 84-year-old recalled.

The ACT portion was leasehold land, while the NSW portion was freehold. Eventually, land acquired for the CSIRO reduced the family’s holding further.

It is one of many stories Kingsley carries from a time when Canberra was still taking shape around farming families who had lived in the district long before the national capital existed.

His family history stretches back to 1838, when his great-grandfather arrived from England. Farming connections in the district date to the 1840s, while Kingsley’s branch of the family occupied its property near Hall from 1877 until he sold it in 2022.

Today, Kingsley lives in Hall, about 10 kilometres from the farm where he spent almost his entire life.

“I was born in Canberra, but I’ve never lived in Canberra,” he said, distinguishing between the capital and the surrounding rural communities.

For him, Hall has always had an identity of its own.

“This place, Hall, is much older than Canberra,” he said, pointing out that the village was proclaimed in 1882, decades before Canberra became the national capital.

But his family’s connection to the district goes back much further.

His great-grandfather arrived in Australia from England in 1838 with his wife and two children. After spending about two years in Sydney, he moved to the Ginninderra district in 1840.

Life in the Australian bush was far from easy. His first wife died following the birth of their ninth child, and the baby also died. He later married a widow with two daughters, and together they had another nine children.

By Kingsley’s reckoning, the combined family numbered 20 children, although one died in infancy.

Those beginnings eventually produced an extensive family network whose history has been carefully recorded for generations. Kingsley still has a remarkable family tree that his mother, Beryl, prepared in 1942.

She gathered the information and commissioned a draftsman to draw the enormous chart, waiting until her son was born so his name could be included. Nearly 85 years later, Kingsley can still unroll the document and point to his place among the many branches. The original became fragile with age, so he had a copy laminated to preserve it.

The family history did not stop there. A Southwell family association continued researching the descendants, compiling books and records that trace the family’s expansion through to 2019.

Kingsley also keeps photographs of his ancestors, including the early family home at Parkwood, in the Ginninderra district, and gatherings held to mark important anniversaries.

In 1938, descendants celebrated 100 years since the family’s arrival in Australia. Another major gathering marked the 150th anniversary in 1988. The family tree has grown considerably, although Kingsley says relatively few descendants still live in Hall.

Kingsley's grandparents

Kingsley's parents

Kinsley's daughter Tarra with her husband.

Kingsley showing his name in the family chart.

Family reunion to mark 100 years in ACT.

Family reunion to mark 150 years in ACT.

His car.

The document that has family tree until 1942

He is now the only Southwell living in the village, although relatives from other branches remain in the district. For much of his life, however, family history was not something kept in books. It was the land he worked every day.

Kingsley was born in 1942 at a private hospital in Forrest. He grew up on the family farm near Hall, where his father raised sheep for wool and kept cattle. As a child, Kingsley attended Hall Primary School, travelling home on his bicycle or catching a mail delivery vehicle that visited farms on Tuesdays and Fridays.

Kingsley would help open farm gates along the way.

With neighbours living considerable distances apart, childhood was largely spent finding his own entertainment.

His mother used to tell him that whoever married him would become “the inventor’s wife”. He loved making things, particularly with his Meccano set, and spent hours experimenting with bits of machinery.

After four years at boarding school in Orange, he returned to work on the family property.

At its peak, his father’s holding was just under 2000 acres. By the time Kingsley was managing it, the property had been reduced to about 1600 acres. The farm carried around 3500 sheep and 150 cattle, with wool providing most of its income.

Kingsley was also a wool classer and took an active role in improving the flock. Unlike his father, who preferred traditional methods, he embraced scientific testing. He would take small wool samples from young sheep, send them to laboratories and use the results to determine which animals should be retained for breeding.

Each sheep had an identification number, allowing him to track its performance.

“By the time it came time to retire, I had a perfect sheep, I thought,” he said.

“But that’s it, to breed sheep, it nearly takes a lifetime.”

Yet even the best breeding could not protect farmers from the collapse in wool prices. Kingsley remembers the boom years of the 1950s, when wool was in strong demand, followed by difficult decades as synthetic fibres gained popularity and the industry struggled with oversupply.

By 1991, conditions had become so desperate that he faced a decision he says still haunts him.

With sheep worth virtually nothing, transporting them to market would have cost more than they could fetch. He and another man gathered 435 sheep into a yard and shot them.

“I shot 435,” he recalled. “Terrible. I cried, I cried, I cried.”

The animals were buried in a dry creek bed. Kingsley said the incident was not unique to his farm. Other woolgrowers were confronting the same devastating conditions. More than three decades later, he still remembers it.

“Still haunts me,” he said.

It was a painful chapter in a farming life that had otherwise been defined by hard work, persistence and a determination to improve the family’s livestock.

There were more ordinary battles too, particularly with rabbits and weeds. Kingsley jokes that he spent more than half his working life trying to control rabbits, watching their numbers fall after disease-control measures only to rise again.

While he worked the land, Canberra was changing around him.

As a boy in the 1940s and 1950s, he remembers his parents travelling to Queanbeyan for banking, shopping, clothing and farm supplies.

Although Canberra had shops, Queanbeyan remained the practical centre for many rural families.

“Canberra back in the 40s, 50s, it was not much of a place,” he said.

The capital’s growth accelerated after World War II, with new suburbs gradually replacing farmland and a growing population changing the character of the district. His children attended schools in Canberra, including St Clare’s College and Marist College. His daughter Tarra now lives in Curtin.

Another son lives in Sydney, while a stepson lives across the Murrumbidgee River. None has followed him into full-time farming. One maintains a small rural property, but Kingsley is quick to distinguish that from earning a living off the land.

Kingsley eventually stepped away from active farming, leasing land to another grazier before selling the property in 2022.

His wife had worked alongside him over the years, even riding a motorbike to help muster livestock. Now retired, the couple live close to the district that has shaped their lives.

Kingsley has mixed feelings about Canberra’s transformation. He appreciates the services the city provides but worries about its growth and believes infrastructure has struggled to keep pace.

He particularly regrets the closure of Hall Primary School, where he once studied.

But the changes also reflect the extraordinary transformation he has witnessed: from a small capital surrounded by working farms to a city whose suburbs, institutions and services now dominate much of the region.

The Southwell family’s connection to the land has changed too. The property is no longer theirs, and the generations who once depended on wool have moved into other professions and cities. Yet their history remains preserved in family photographs, books and the enormous chart Kingsley’s mother commissioned in 1942. He can still trace the line from the English migrant who arrived in 1838, through the farming generations that followed, to his own place in the family.

The border that once divided their land may have changed hands, and the farm itself may have passed to others, but nearly two centuries of family history remain firmly connected to the Canberra region.

canberra.title: Hackett residents call for pause on public housing DA, launch petition
canberra.snippet: Hackett residents concerned about a public housing proposal in their suburb have called on the ACT Government to pause the development ap...
canberra.content:
25 November 2026

Start the conversation

The Hackett community meeting. The concern was around the inadequacy of the design. Photo: Liam Jones.

Hackett residents concerned about a public housing proposal in their suburb have called on the ACT Government to pause the development application.

About 80 people gathered at Hackett Oval for a community meeting about the proposed public housing development at Holtze Close and Madigan Street.

The $6.6 million supportive housing proposal is for a three-storey, 14-metre-high building that will sit on a one-level, 33-space basement carpark and comprise 27 units. A single-storey waste enclosure and a new substation are also included.

Two blocks are involved: one is the site of the former ESA depot, and the other is a treed bit of green space next to Hackett Oval.

In line with the government’s commitment to expedite more social housing, the proposal has been designated a Territory Priority Project, precluding any third-party appeals.

Residents are upset about the scale of the proposal and lack of consultation, but insist they are not opposed to public housing.

Residents heard at the meeting that the government had been working on the proposal for two years, yet the community was given just three weeks to make submissions, since extended to four.

Local MLAs Elizabeth Lee (Liberal) and Rebecca Vassarotti (ACT Greens) attended the meeting, along with representatives from the offices of Independent MLA Thomas Emerson and Deputy Chief Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith.

The major concern aired was that the proposed design was insufficient, did not meet community expectations and that Hackett residents had not been given any opportunity to provide input.

An illustration of the proposed Hackett public housing complex. Image: Our Architect.

There was also concern that no new community services have been identified to support the number of future residents, many of whom may need additional support.

Several residents also queried the proposed car parking standards, the completeness of the development application documents, and whether the proposal met Territory planning guidelines and legislative requirements.

Potential threats to endangered species habitat, including the gang-gang cockatoo, and the environmental impacts of removing established and protected trees were also raised.

Spokesperson Liam Jones said Hackett was an inclusive suburb that was up for a conversation about new public housing.

“This isn’t about whether public housing belongs in our suburb. It’s about getting it right for the people who will live here and those who will live in the housing, and that starts with talking to the community,” he said.

“We are calling on the ACT Government to pause its process until the community has been properly consulted and new design options can be developed with the community. We want to work constructively with the government to get this right.”

A petition sponsored by Ms Lee has been launched requesting the Legislative Assembly to call on the government to pause or withdraw the DA until the Hackett community has been properly consulted; consult the community on the future use of the land; and commit to developing new design options with the community, before the DA or any replacement application proceeds.

Organisers hope the petition can attract more than 500 signatures and instigate a committee inquiry.

canberra.title: Aptly named racehorse smashes track record, helps fund Canberra palliative care
canberra.snippet: New Zealand-bred thoroughbred gelding I’mintowin took just over one minute and 20 seconds to smash the track record at Thoroughbred...
canberra.content:
25 November 2026

Start the conversation

Palliative Care ACT will make big strides with the windfall from its Canberra Community Chest win, thanks to Thoroughbred Park and an aptly named racehorse. Photo: Claire Xiao.

New Zealand-bred thoroughbred gelding I’mintowin took just over one minute and 20 seconds to smash the track record at Thoroughbred Park. For the people Palliative Care ACT supports, the $25,000 that galloped across the finish line with him will leave a legacy.

The windfall from taking out the 2026 Canberra Community Chest is going straight into the charity’s A Moment in Time program, an initiative that records the voices, stories and final messages of Canberrans approaching the end of their lives so their families have something permanent to hold on to.

With $25,000 in the bank, Palliative Care ACT can now fund more than 300 of those recordings, or provide training to expand the program from audio keepsakes to video.

Palliative Care ACT CEO Paul Artzenhofer said the team was stunned as their equine hero crossed the line first.

“We were all in shock and almost disbelief that I’mintowin won, and so convincingly,” he said. “The shocked looks on our faces said it all.”

The Canberra Community Chest is an annual charity race run by the Canberra Racing Club at Thoroughbred Park, pairing 12 local charities and community groups with 12 racehorses to compete for what is typically a $50,000 prize pool. This year, that total was boosted to $65,000 thanks to a contribution from the Canberra Southern Cross Club.

Toora Women Incorporated finished second with Well Timed, securing $8500, while Helping ACT placed third with Sandpaper to take home $6000. Every partner walked away with at least $2500, including Pam’s Pantry, whose tenth-place finish still gave the team plenty to smile about.

“The prize money means Pam’s Pantry can reach more families with food vouchers, Christmas gifts and a bit more Lego for the older children,” Pam’s Pantry founder Pamela Zieke said.

The race was thrilling, with I’mintowin smashing the track record. Photo: Claire Xiao.

But wins from the Community Chest transcended funding alone, by bringing charities together. Paul noted Palliative Care ACT’s plans to collaborate with Win The Day, Pegasus and Good Omen Goodeze.

“In the community sector you can often feel like you are on your own, but this week has reminded us of that true sense of community,” Paul said.

“If you’re on the fence about applying (for the Canberra Community Chest), do it.

“I have already started receiving help from other charities, including half a van load of brand new toys from Rise Above,” Pamela added.

“Pam’s Pantry is definitely going to apply again next year. It is an amazing way to meet many other charities, and the staff made sure everyone was looked after.”

The Canberra Community Chest has distributed $215,000 to partner organisations since launching in 2023.

Thoroughbred Park’s Robbie Ringland said the 2026 instalment was the ideal first race-day experience for many newcomers to Thoroughbred Park.

“The mood was celebratory, welcoming and inclusive … There was a lot of excitement, especially when our three winners stood up there. It was pretty emotional, to be honest,” he said.

“The Canberra Community Chest is my favourite of all our race days because of that deep community element. It connects us to 12 awesome organisations with important causes, and each of our winners shared the very impactful, tangible ways their winnings would go towards helping families doing it tough.”

The mood at Thoroughbred Park for the Canberra Community Chest was celebratory, welcoming and inclusive. Photo: Claire Xiao.

The winners of the 2026 Canberra Community Chest are:

  • 1st: I’mintowin (NZ) — Palliative Care ACT ($25,000)
  • 2nd: Well Timed — Toora Women Incorporated ($8,500)
  • 3rd: Sandpaper — Helping ACT ($6,000)
  • 4th: Brave Xena — Equine Pathways Australia ($4,000)
  • 5th: Alabama State — Rise Above ($3,500)
  • 6th: Asgarda — ACT Volunteer Brigades ($3,000)
  • 7th: Deepwater Artist (NZ) — Good Omen Goodeze ($2,500)
  • 8th: Felix Majestic — Win The Day Charity ($2,500)
  • 9th: Geemes — Pegasus Riding For The Disabled ($2,500)
  • 10th: I’ve Bean Tryin’ — Pam’s Pantry ($2,500)
  • 11th: Graceful Ellen — See Yourself ($2,500)
  • 12th: Hot Bandit — Formally Formal Wear ($2,500).

canberra.title: Still no answers on what caused Triple Zero outage to ambulance, fire services
canberra.snippet: The ACT’s Emergency Services Agency head has promised full transparency as work continues to determine what caused a Triple Zero ou...
canberra.content:
25 November 2026

Start the conversation

ACT ESA Commissioner Wayne Phillips said investigations were continuing into what caused a Triple Zero outage and why backup systems didn’t work as expected. Photo: Thomas Lucraft.

The ACT’s Emergency Services Agency head has promised full transparency as work continues to determine what caused a Triple Zero outage and why the backup systems didn’t work as expected.

At 8:11 pm on Thursday (19 November), power was lost to the ESA’s Fairbairn communications centre for four minutes, causing four in-progress Triple Zero calls to drop out.

The first backup battery system didn’t work, and it took four minutes for the second backup system to kick in.

ACT ESA Commissioner Wayne Phillips said investigations were still underway into what caused the outage, why the first backup system didn’t work, and why there was a lag in the second system’s operation.

“[The second system] is expected to kick in … straight away,” he said.

“Once we know exactly what happened, I’ll be transparent about what occurred, how it occurred, and what our steps are then to rectify it and make it even better.”

The agency is working with the Digital Canberra Directorate to identify the root cause of the issues.

The communications centre has a backup facility in Hume, which was brought online as a contingency response.

Staff worked out of that centre from Thursday evening until Sunday morning, and are now back at the Fairbairn site.

Commissioner Phillips was proud of how the contingency plans had worked.

“Our people, [the] call takers online at the time … [were] able to get [those dropped calls] back, to keep business going, pack up a comms centre, move the comms centre seamlessly, on Thursday night,” he said.

“It’s fantastic work done by both our paramedic ambulance call takers and our firefighter call takers … it shows that we have a resilient Triple Zero network.”

No other calls were received during the outage.

If people had tried to call emergency fire or ambulance services, they would have been diverted to ACT Policing’s call centre.

canberra.title: Council staff member allegedly ‘brutally’ stomped on and killed duckling at Queanbeyan Pool
canberra.snippet: Multiple investigations are underway after a duckling was allegedly killed by a council staff member at Queanbeyan Pool. Queanbeyan-Paler...
canberra.content:
The allegedly killed duckling was one of 10 babies for the Queanbeyan Pool wood duck family. Photo: Facebook/Ross Macdonald.

Multiple investigations are underway after a duckling was allegedly killed by a council staff member at Queanbeyan Pool.

Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council councillor Ross Macdonald confirmed the incident.

“Allegedly an animal was euthanised by a staff member,” he said.

The QPRC general manager informed all councillors late last week about the alleged incident.

“Council acted quickly once the allegation was made, and the staff member or members involved were immediately stood down,” Mr Macdonald said.

The four-week-old duckling was part of a wood duck family known to visit the facility.

It had been seen struggling to keep up with the rest of its family, and Wildcare was given a call on 11 November.

“The lifeguards at the pool … were worried about this little one,” volunteer Melissa Pearce said.

It was found that both the duckling’s ankles were wrapped in fine strands of cotton that had ended up embedded in the tissue.

Ms Pearce managed to remove the strings and gave the duckling pain relief.

But it wasn’t coping on its own.

“It was very stressed; ducklings don’t do well on their own,” Ms Pearce explained.

Overnight, the duckling’s recovery went well – it was eating, defecating and able to walk with a slight limp.

The decision was made to return the duckling to its family at Queanbeyan Pool.

“I felt it was fairly safe place for it to be … protected from cars and foxes and things like that,” Ms Pearce said.

The pool’s lifeguards continued to take photos of the duckling and share its recovery progress with Wildcare.

The family was also featured in social media posts promoting the pool’s upcoming 65th anniversary.

Ms Pearce had planned on visiting the pool on Friday (20 November) to check on its progress in person.

But on Thursday (19 November) night she received a “distressing” message from one of the lifeguards.

It appeared concerns had grown about the duckling’s foot and ability to survive, so the pool manager allegedly had taken the situation into her own hands.

It’s alleged she asked another staff member for assistance before catching the duckling.

“They took it out the back to stomp on it,” Ms Pearce said.

“They then put it in a plastic bag and put it in the bin.”

Ms Pearce said several of the teenage lifeguards immediately emailed their boss’s manager to raise their concerns.

“One of the young lifeguards very bravely and sadly removed the duckling from the garbage bin, took some photos and video, and buried it,” she said.

“It really sad thing is … if they were concerned about [the duckling’s] welfare, the staff had my number.

“It did not need to be killed by having someone brutally stomp on its head.”

It is illegal in NSW to harm, euthanise or catch native wildlife in order to keep them as pets.

Ms Pearce emphasised this fact.

“People shouldn’t take it upon themselves to care for or euthanise injured wildlife,” she said.

“I might have had a look [at the duckling and decided] the kindest thing to do was euthanasia, and taken it to the local vet.

“But we’re never going to know.”

It’s understood the NSW Biodiversity and Heritage Regulator is investigating the alleged incident.

Mr Macdonald understood the community would be disturbed by the allegations from Queanbeyan Pool.

“As a person in the community, as a councillor and as a Wildcare volunteer, the allegations are shocking and saddening,” he said.

“I can understand people in the community would be shocked … [but] I encourage people to allow the investigations to continue, and not hypothesise or make suggestions which are unhelpful.”

Ms Pearce also wanted to commend the actions of the pool lifeguards, not only for caring for the duckling while it was recovering, but for speaking up when they witnessed the alleged killing.

“Those young people spoke up and advocated and shared their concerns with council and Wildcare and the NSW Biodiversity investigators,” she said.

“It’s not easy to do when you’re 16 or 17 years old.”

Region understands Queanbeyan Pool was shut for a short time on Tuesday (24 November) for staff to receive support.

Original Article published by Claire Fenwicke on About Regional.

australia.title: Auditors accused of falsifying work as Asic publishes ‘shameful list of failures’
australia.snippet: Deloitte, EY, PricewaterhouseCoopers and KPMG subject of Australian corporate regulator review of employee complaints Get our daily polit...
australia.content:
A review has found Australia’s big four auditors have been accused by employees of failings including falsifying work, covering up concerns and possibly manipulating audit findings.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic) urged sweeping reform when it published its report on Wednesday, as the Albanese government considers new regulations on the firms.

The corporate regulator found 35 key allegations of misconduct in audits since 2023 when it reviewed Deloitte, EY, PricewaterhouseCoopers and KPMG. The latter firm is also battling a scandal over integrity failures that saw the chief executive quit and which prompted the Asic probe.

Asic did not disclose which allegations related to which firm and the firms declined to clarify when contacted.

Deborah O’Neill, a Labor senator and chair of the committee that exposed KPMG’s failings, said the review was a “shameful list of failures”.

“It’s clearer than ever that the barrel contains more than just a few bad apples,” O’Neill said.

Combined, the four firms audit the finances of almost all of Australia’s top listed companies. Statutory audits are legally required for sharemarket-listed businesses and other big companies.

After KPMG this year admitted to inappropriately sharing clients’ confidential information then dismissing an employee’s complaints, Asic began reviewing the four firms’ complaints from 2023 to 2026.

It found 35 serious complaints with the most common being that work was falsified, or documented incorrectly or without evidence. Staff were accused of using misleading documentation as evidence, recording details without verifying them and claiming that tests were completed when they never occurred.

Other complaints alleged staff breached confidentiality, gave incorrect audit instructions and potentially attempted to manipulate audits’ conclusions, Asic said.

Issues such as bullying, sexual harassment and sending sensitive information to personal email accounts accounted for the other 523 audit-related complaints.

While the regulator identified numerous concerns for audit quality, it said only one of the complaints had its investigation reopened.

Some allegations were formally investigated and substantiated, with firms sacking or replacing staff, redoing audits and issuing warnings.

But Asic warned firms did not seem to have checked whether what people found in one audit had recurred in others. Reviews were typically led by HR teams and sometimes focused on alleged bullying or workload problems while ignoring audit-related issues.

Other complainants alleged they faced retaliation for speaking up. Firms in some cases dismissed credible complaints over a lack of documentary evidence, Asic said.

‘Out of line’

Asic said the big four attempted to limit its access to information surrounding the complaints, taking a “protracted and legalistic” approach.

“The majority of firms responded by withholding or redacting documents, making extensive legal professional privilege claims, missing required deadlines, and prioritising their own internal investigations,” the report read.

“This was out of line with our expectations and experience with other sectors.”

Behaviour only improved when Asic wrote to the firms’ chairs, it said.

KPMG had previously attempted to limit parliament’s access to its whistleblower investigations until its chairman, Martin Sheppard, backflipped under pressure from the parliamentary committee. Sheppard resigned days later, following multiple other top executives, while the chief operating officer was sacked and is suing the firm.

The federal government blacklisted KPMG from its contracts until at least March, with a report for the department of finance estimating the firm has lost $31m worth of contracts. KPMG has cut hundreds of jobs in response to lost income.

Contacted for comment, KPMG said it was committed to audit quality and was considering how Asic’s report could help as it worked to improve its management of complaints and protection of whistle blowers.

PwC, which faced its own tax leaks scandal in 2023, said it was continuously improving its processes and supported stronger surveillance and enforcement.

Deloitte and EY, which have not suffered recent scandals, said they welcomed the review and had strong processes for handling and disclosing complaints.

The Albanese government in July consulted on reforms which would put the firms under the corporate regulator’s direct oversight, which Asic commissioner Kate O’Rourke welcomed on Wednesday.

Barbara Pocock, a Greens senator and member of the parliamentary committee, said the report showed “massive culture problems” were “rife”.

“We need a regulator with teeth to hold them to account for their gross misdemeanours,” Pocock said.

A spokeswoman for the assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, said the government response to the consultation was in progress and would be released “in due course”.

australia.title: Chinese police contacted members of WeChat group after they discussed Melbourne vigil for HungryPanda rider
australia.snippet: Several members of the group chat set up after the alleged murder of Feng Jianming say they or their parents were called by police from t...
australia.content:
Chinese police have contacted several people who were part of a WeChat group that discussed attending a Melbourne vigil for Feng Jianming, the HungryPanda food delivery rider allegedly murdered earlier this month.

At least three members of the group set up after Feng’s death said they were contacted, raising concerns that Chinese authorities may have been alerted to discussions about the protest activity either automatically or manually by the Chinese-owned messaging and social app.

Feng was allegedly stabbed to death near Queen Victoria market on the evening of Friday 6 November after he and another rider confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes.

Angry members of the WeChat group set up in the immediate aftermath volunteered to host a vigil for the 49-year-old rider at the State Library of Victoria the following day, amid broader concerns about the treatment of riders by the company.

The group’s chat history, seen by the Guardian, shows that by Wednesday at least three members had told the group their parents or themselves had been called by police officers from their home towns in China asking about their involvement with the vigil. The group, which by then had more than 400 members, was disbanded the following day after participants expressed fears about the police calls.

Members of the chat group declined to speak on the record, citing safety concerns.

HungryPanda, founded in the UK, targets the Chinese expatriate market in 10 countries. In Australia, it operates in nine cities, including Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide.

The Melbourne incident mirrored an event in February when HungryPanda riders in Sydney were contacted by police from China after a WeChat discussion about a proposed strike over wages on lunar new year’s eve.

More than half the WeChat group’s 155 members left and the strike was abandoned after the calls from police, which were first reported by the ABC.

Joy Wang, a former HungryPanda rider who was in the February group chat, said she received four police calls from her home town in Henan province.

Wang said the police seemed unaware the protest was in Sydney. When she explained this, they threatened her with reprisals if she went back to China, she said.

“They said, ‘You better not attend the protest, or we could go after you when you return to China’,” Wang said.

Jack*, who quit HungryPanda two years ago and now runs his own business in eastern China, said he joined the February WeChat group to show support to his former colleagues. He received three calls from police in his home town and was told not to take part in the strike.

Jack then quit the group chat. “I’m currently in China, there are things I need to consider,” he said.

Kitty Lu, global spokeswoman for HungryPanda, said the company had no responsibility for riders being contacted by Chinese police. The company was privately owned and independently operated, with funding from private and institutional investors in Europe and North America, she said.

Wang said the group members in Australia who were called by police had registered with WeChat under their Chinese mobile numbers.

She believed the use of keywords such as “strike” in the chat may have been the trigger for the messages to be transmitted to the Chinese authorities.

Jeffrey Knockel, a senior research fellow at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, agreed. He and his colleagues studied a 2016 wage protest in Jiangsu province and found the phrase “industrial strike across the city” in the organisers’ group chat activated an automated mechanism on WeChat.

He suggested something similar may have happened in the Australian cases. Knockel also argued that WeChat may have flagged the group chat to a Chinese government organisation that would have then traced the riders’ details on China’s family registration system, known as hukou, and instructed local police to contact them.

WeChat has previously stated that the data of foreign users is stored in Singapore, beyond the reach of Chinese authorities, but Knockel said that if one member of a group registered their account with a Chinese number, the whole chat could be monitored by Chinese authorities.

WeChat did not respond to a request for comment.

Kevin Slaten, who leads the China Dissent Monitor at the US-based thinktank Freedom House, also thought the February calls might have been triggered by WeChat, given a rise in the number of labour disputes over wages in China during 2025 and early 2026.

“[The Chinese authorities may have] just assumed that these workers were in this wave of wage protests … not knowing initially that they weren’t physically located in China,” Slaten said.

But as the security apparatus was under direction to pay special attention to wage protests, the police may have persisted in warning riders to halt their action, even after learning they were overseas, he said.

The executive director of China Labor Watch, Qiang Li, has documented several cases of Chinese workers abroad being contacted by Chinese authorities after using WeChat to discuss industrial action. However, these workers were usually working for projects by China’s state companies.

Li said Chinese police had “overreacted” in the HungryPanda case but it was still alarming for Australia.

“Today we see these riders being called by Chinese police,” he said. “We could then see cases of anyone who uses WeChat, including Australian enforcement officials, their families, or anyone related to China, to be surveilled through this system.”

The home affairs department said it could not comment on operational matters but a spokesperson said it was “unacceptable for any foreign government to target members of our community to prevent individuals exercising their fundamental rights and freedoms in Australia”.

“Acts of harassment, assault, unwanted surveillance, intimidation, coercion or other threatening behaviour may constitute criminal offences.”

The opposition home affairs spokesman, Jonathon Duniam, called on the government to do more to address the potential use of WeChat for surveillance.

“The Coalition has raised serious concerns about WeChat’s links to the Chinese Communist party, its censorship practices and its potential use for surveillance, yet the Albanese government has not done enough to address these risks or ensure proper transparency and accountability from the platform,” he said.

In 2023, a Senate inquiry into foreign interference recommended banning WeChat on government devices and establishing a national security technology office to monitor “high-risk” social media groups, including WeChat.

The government said only that it “noted” these recommendations.

The Chinese embassy in Canberra declined to comment on the HungryPanda allegations.

australia.title: Guardian Essential poll: Albanese’s disapproval rating hits highest level as problems mount for Labor
australia.snippet: Australians also turn against AI datacentres, with nearly half saying they don’t want one near their home Get our daily political email ,...
australia.content:
Anthony Albanese’s approval ratings have nosedived in the latest Guardian Essential poll, with the prime minister reaching his highest level of disapproval after his net popularity plummeted 10 points in just a month.

Australians have also turned strongly against AI datacentres, with nearly half of the country saying they don’t want one near their home. Women, older people and One Nation and Greens supporters are among the most likely to reject living near a datacentre.

This month’s Guardian Essential poll, of 1,087 people taken last week, found a tightening political horse race amid mounting political problems for the Labor government. Labor and One Nation remain deadlocked, both with a primary vote of 26%, each having registered a slight dip since both last month recorded 28%. The Coalition’s fortunes have improved slightly, moving to 25%, up from last month’s 23%, while the Greens are on 13%.

The biggest shift in November’s poll is a sudden collapse in the approval ratings for the prime minister. Just 32% of Australians approved of his job performance, down from 38% last month, while simultaneously 60% of people disapproved of Albanese, up from last month’s 56%.

That’s a net approval rating of minus-28, a 10-point fall since October.

Albanese’s approval rating has never been lower, and his disapproval rating has never been higher, since becoming prime minister. Even after ferocious criticism and scrutiny of the government after the Bondi terror shooting last December, Albanese recorded a 39% approval and 53% disapproval in January.

The collapse in Albanese’s personal ratings comes as cost-of-living pressures continue to bite the government, with scrutiny on Labor’s spending priorities and economic record amid high petrol prices and rising interest rates. Albanese has also come under personal attack from opponents over budget decisions, comments on podcasts and grants funding. The poll was taken last week, while Albanese was overseas at the Cop31 climate conference and international summits in Asia.

“No one wins popularity points on the global stage, particularly when living costs are high. But worse for the PM was his proximity to the dysfunction that global affairs has become, with Cop collapsing and then playing second fiddle at Yalta 2.0,” said Peter Lewis, the chair of Essential Media.

“A chance for a break and a reset can’t come fast enough for him.”

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, recorded a 35% approval and 42% disapproval, which has remained largely unchanged for several months.

Essential also probed Australians’ views on datacentres, finding a significant negative shift in sentiment around the AI factories.

Following a major rise in opposition to datacentres at the American midterm elections, Essential found only 23% of Australians would support having one near their home, with 48% against.

That compares to 28% in favour and 37% opposed in July, the last time Essential asked this question. In just four months, Australians’ support for living near a datacentre has swung 16% to the negative.

“The deterioration in support for datacentres follows successful community campaigns against local developments, as well as a string of AI-related job cuts. The datacentre becomes an avatar for all the unresolved issues around the regulation and scale of this technology,” Lewis said.

Asked for their major concerns about datacentres, the most commonly cited worry was around impacts on energy demand and electricity prices (61% of people), local water supply (54%) and impact on the environment (39%). Some 38% of people voiced general worries about the growth of AI.

Broken down by demographic, women (55% oppose) were much less likely than men (40% oppose) to support living near a datacentre. Views get more negative as Australians get older, with 57% of over-55s against living near one, compared to 37% of 18-34s and 47% of 35-54s.

Greens (59% oppose) and One Nation (53% oppose) supporters were far more negative on datacentres than Labor and Liberal voters (both 42% oppose).

australia.title: Days out from the Victorian election, nine datacentre projects await approval. What will their fate be?
australia.snippet: While parties have come out with policies on where datacentres can be built, not all are clear on whether they apply retrospectively Get ...
australia.content:
Days out from the Victorian state election, the fate of nine datacentre projects remains uncertain, with some companies confident they will be able to get their projects across the line after Saturday.

There are nine datacentre projects currently awaiting approval according to the ministerial permits register, including the West Footscray expansion of NextDC’s M3 datacentre, which Guardian Australia reported has faced delays due to community blowback.

Other companies seeking approval for new datacentres include ZerraDC, HyperDC, GreenSquareDC, and Stockland.

The GreenSquareDC proposal for a $1.5bn, 240MW datacentre encompassing more than 105,000 sq metres of Spotswood in Melbourne’s inner west has faced strong opposition from locals similar to that observed in other suburbs around the country.

The proposal was lodged with the minister for planning at the end of July this year, but as with the other projects, it did not get approval before the government went into caretaker mode before the election.

A spokesperson for GreenSquareDC said the proposed development was on a long-vacant site in an established industrial precinct in Spotswood, and the company was proud of its proposal.

“We’ll work constructively with whichever government Victorians elect, and we’ll keep engaging with the Spotswood community throughout the process.”

Locals, however, have mobilised, with a petition with more than 4,400 signatures, and a dedicated website that encourages residents to contact the current planning minister and outlines the various policies on datacentres held by candidates in the Williamstown electorate.

The policies

Last month, after launching the Labor policy in September, the Victorian planning minister, Sonya Kilkenny, released a statement of expectations for applications submitted on or after 23 September.

It includes that datacentres must be built away from homes, schools, and childcare centres, and that they must be designed and located to minimise impact on residential communities.

Developments would be prohibited from residential zones, or within 150m of accommodation, education centres or hospitals, as well as green wedge zones (areas preserved for housing or agriculture), rural zones, or urban growth zones.

Exceptions on the latter are made if it is within 5km of a powerline or substation operating at 66,000 volts, or most of the electricity is supplied from either a renewable energy facility or a battery energy storage system.

Developers will be required to display prominent signage onsite and publish detailed application documentation online.

A spokesperson for the Coalition said datacentres would not be built in residential areas, next to residential areas, or in the green wedge.

“Datacentres will be an important part of Victoria’s future,” the spokesperson said. “They drive investment, create skilled jobs and build the sovereign capability our state needs in a digital economy.”

There would be designated datacentre precincts distanced from where people live, and clear guidelines on where they can and cannot be built, the spokesperson said.

“That means communities can have confidence their neighbourhoods are protected, and investors can have confidence about where to build.”

The Liberal policy does not outline whether the plans apply retrospectively, and makes no statement on power requirements.

The Victorian Greens have a policy of a moratorium on new datacentre developments “until communities have actually had an opportunity to consider the risks and benefits, and create strong laws to protect people and the planet over big tech profit”.

The party’s policy also calls for compensation for affected communities, reverting the fast-track approval process to give communities a greater say, and ensuring datacentres are 100% renewables-powered.

One Nation’s policies call for a ban on new datacentres on agricultural land, as well as a call for full community impact assessments before approval.

The party has also said there will be no retrospective carve-outs, so residents living next to a proposed or expanding datacentre will have the same rights as those living near new developments.

The party has also outlined that datacentres would need to be at an undefined distance from homes.

Developers confident ahead of the election

NextDC chief executive, Craig Scroggie, said in a shareholder update in late October that despite the issues with power supply to the datacentre, he had no reason to believe the expansion would not be approved after the election.

“Even with the revised changes to planning guidelines, they do not apply to existing applications that are already being considered by the planning minister.”

“This caretaker period will ultimately result in a new government being appointed [and a] new minister. We would therefore take the conservative view that given what we understand currently about the government’s approval processes and the upcoming election that the time we would be able to restart that [would be] February or later, depending on the election.”

Sean Brown, a West Footscray resident and Citizens of Tottenham member, told Guardian Australia last month the community would make its voice heard to the incoming planning minister after Saturday.

“We’re not stopping. This is continuing until we get a fair outcome for the residents,” he said.

“It will be a pretty toxic thing to sign off on.”

DoverDC, which is planning a $2.6bn 200MW datacentre next to AusNet’s South Morang terminal station, said its project would be assessed on its merits regardless of the election outcome.

“It is on this basis that it was accepted into the planning process by the current state government and we see no reason why that should change,” a spokesperson said.

Goodman Group, which has lodged plans for three two-storey datacentre buildings in Truganina, west of Melbourne, said it would not speculate on the election outcome or the planning decision but would work constructively with the government and local community.

world.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
world.snippet: Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa When the ...
world.content:
When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.

“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”

The Kremlin-controlled forces and their Malian allies were facing a coordinated surprise assault by the al-Qaida-linked JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), whose fighters used suicide car bombs and drones to break through the city’s defences.

Leaked Russian state records suggest the losses were heavy that day. Death certificates of Russian fighters killed in Mali, held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, were obtained by the hacker groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow and analysed by the Guardian.

The records show that 43 Russians died in Mali on 25 April, including six in Kidal and one in nearby Aguelhok. Others were recorded as dying in the capital, Bamako, and in Gao, where rebels shot down a Russian military helicopter that day.

By the following morning, the Russians had abandoned Kidal, which Russian mercenaries had helped capture in November 2023 and which Moscow had since held up as a showcase of its growing influence in Africa.

In all, the records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026, most of which the Guardian was able to link to known battles with rebel groups.

The figures offer a previously unseen glimpse into the human cost of Moscow’s efforts to prop up Mali’s military junta, in what has become Russia’s largest military deployment in Africa.

Two western officials who have travelled to Mali and were shown the data said the death toll was higher than previously estimated.

“That’s over 10% of Russia’s forces killed in action,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.

Moscow does not publish its losses in Africa, and its foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The Wagner private military group, led by the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin, first arrived in Mali in late 2021, a year after a military coup had toppled President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. French forces were ordered to leave the country as relations with the junta deteriorated, bringing an end to France’s decade-long counter-terrorism operation and leaving Russia as the regime’s main foreign protector.

Wagner handed over its operations in Mali to the Africa Corps in June 2025, two years after Prigozhin led a failed mutiny on Moscow that discredited the group in the eyes of the Kremlin. By that summer, British intelligence estimated that about 2,000 Africa Corps personnel were deployed in the country.

The Africa Corps, closely overseen by Russian military intelligence, currently provides backing to several African governments in return for payment or lucrative contracts granting access to natural resources.

Despite the Russian presence, Mali’s security situation has continued to deteriorate. In late July 2024, Russian and Malian forces fought Tuareg separatists for several days near Tinzaouaten, on the Algerian border.

Wagner at the time issued a rare statement admitting losses, including the death of a commander, but gave no figure. Estimates from Russian sources ranged from about 20 to more than 80 dead.

The Rosstat records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July 2024, all but one of them in the Kidal region. The figures make the battle of Tinzaouaten the deadliest single day for Russian forces in Africa since Wagner mercenaries first deployed to the continent in 2017.

The toll in Mali may have been driven up by Ukraine, which has extended its war against Russia to the Sahel. Kyiv has been assisting Tuareg rebels there, according to two people with knowledge of the operations. CNN has reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed to Mali to help local rebel forces fighting Russian troops.

The records are probably an undercount. Registration often lags, and no Russian deaths in Mali are recorded for March 2026 although at least three Africa Corps fighters were reported killed in an ambush near Nampala that month.

The leaked data also sheds light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa. Central African Republic, where Wagner fighters guard the president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, accounts for 30 deaths. While not all could be linked to known incidents, three men died on the night drones struck Wagner camps in Kaga-Bandoro in December 2023.

In Libya, where Russian forces back the eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and use his airbases as a supply route to their deployments in the Sahel, some of the recorded deaths were probably linked to a helicopter crash at the Maaten al-Sarra base in February 2026. On Sunday, Ukrainian drones sunk a Russian warship off the coast of Libya; it is unclear whether there were any casualties.

In Niger, where Russia’s Africa Corps moved in after the military junta expelled French and US troops, a Russian fighter died two days after Islamic State militants attacked Niamey airport in January, a previously unreported casualty.

Moscow has in recent months stepped up its effort to show it is back in control in Mali. On 6 October, Malian troops and the Africa Corps recaptured Kidal after what the army called an air and ground campaign.

A report this month by the US-based Conflict Insights Group (CIG) found that the Africa Corps had sharply increased its use of drones in Mali, including Lancet suicide drones, amid an intensifying air campaign.

The group wrote that the drone campaign had also targeted civilians, boostering support for the rebels. “Civilian deaths in the intensified air campaign, which the Africa Corps leads, are likely to aid insurgent recruitment,” it said.


A western diplomat who works in the region said the attacks in late April had punctured the image of Russian military invincibility that Moscow and the junta had cultivated among Malians.

“Russia still wields considerable influence in Mali, but patience with its military performance is wearing thin.”

world.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
world.snippet: Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship Ukraine has confirmed i...
world.content:
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.

Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.

“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”

Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Institute for the Study of War said the Merkury had stopped over for several days, under a cooperation agreement, to refuel and resupply as it escorted Russian cargo ships that could carry military supplies en route to Russia.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.

Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts to use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.

The confirmation that Ukraine was behind the attacks was condemned by the UN-recognised government in Tripoli. It said Libya rejected ⁠any foreign ⁠military ​operations on its territory or in its waters.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.

Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, said Ukraine’s strikes in the Mediterranean “were exceptionally brazen and provocative”.

He added: “The question now is how Russia will retaliate,. Perhaps even more pressing is how the [Hafter] family will respond, given how traumatic the scale of the destruction has been for eastern Libyan authorities.”

Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

world.title: Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack
world.snippet: No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia A Russian warship docked in th...
world.content:
A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.

The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.

Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.

Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine, marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.

Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.

Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion.

Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the vessel’s crew, the ‌sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.

Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.

There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.

The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the two drone attacks off Benghazi and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.

The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.

It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.

“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.

HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.

If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.

But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.

On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.

The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

world.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
world.snippet: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded Multiple coastal hazard warnings we...
world.content:
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

world.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
world.snippet: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Afri...
world.content:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”

Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.

A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.
